extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, educated general readers and scientists interested in human evolution and comparative anatomy
extracted.subtask_description: Darwin's argumentation about how natural selection, sexual selection, use and disuse, correlation, and other causes could have produced distinctive human anatomical and mental traits. The text gives criteria for attributing features of humans (bipedalism, hands, brain size, nakedness, tail loss, etc.) to these processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for natural selection to act on man
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is variable in body and mind; variations are induced by the same general causes and obey the same laws as with lower animals. Man has spread widely and been exposed to diversified conditions; his progenitors tended to increase beyond their means of subsistence and were exposed to a struggle for existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beneficial variations will be preserved and injurious ones eliminated; this applies to mere individual differences as well as to larger deviations. Examples: muscles of hands and feet are liable to incessant variability; the half of a population better adapted for movement or defense would on average survive and procreate more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence that a trait can be explained by natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications in structure or constitution that serve to adapt an organism to its habits of life, to the food it consumes, or passively to surrounding conditions may have been acquired through natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, modifications that do not serve to adapt an organism to these ends cannot have been thus acquired. Be cautious: many functions are unknown and correlation/secondary effects may confound attribution. Use comparisons across taxa, observations of function, and consideration of correlated changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of correlated variation and secondary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of correlation: many strange deviations of structure are tied together, and a change in one part often leads, through increased or decreased use of other parts, to unexpected changes in those parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an adaptation, account for correlated modifications and indirect effects (examples: galls caused by insects, plumage changes in parrots from diet/toxins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of use and inherited effects of use/disuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes caused by increased or decreased use of certain parts may be inherited and thus contribute to structural change along with natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for habitual enlargement of muscles and associated bone crests as evidence of habitual use leading to selection for those actions; consider experimental or observed transmitted effects (Darwin cites cases such as inherited effects of mutilations in some animals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humans' dominance explained by intellectual, social, and corporeal characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Man's pre-eminent success in the struggle for life is due to his intellectual faculties, social habits which lead to mutual aid and defense, and his corporeal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue importance of these characters by their final arbitrament in the battle for life; e.g., intellectual faculties led to language and inventions (weapons, tools, fire) that conferred survival advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive explanation for bipedalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Becoming erect or bipedal would be advantageous if it freed the hands and arms for prehension, tool-using and defense, allowed firmer stance for throwing or using weapons, and improved ability to obtain food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection would favor the best-built (more erect) individuals; intermediate forms need not be maladapted, as illustrated by existing anthropomorphous apes that show intermediate modes of progression (e.g., gorilla shambling gait, apes using arms as crutches). Consider correlated changes required (pelvis, spine curvature, head position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of physiological labour as an explanatory principle
rubrics_metrics.description: As hands became perfected for prehension, the feet should become perfected for support and locomotion; specialization of appendages follows the division of physiological labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative anatomy and functional considerations (e.g., flat feet, modification of great toe) to evaluate adaptive hypotheses about limb specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand structure and tool use as criteria for selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A hand capable of precise hammering, accurate throwing, fine sense of touch and manipulating small objects confers major mechanical advantages and would be strongly selected for; primeval men practising division of labour and tool manufacture implies selection for manual dexterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare primate hands: similarity of pattern but differences in prehensile specialization (climbing vs manipulation) indicate adaptive trade-offs. Evidence: archaeological inference about long intervals before grinding chipped flints into polished tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of jaws and canines via reduced use and weapon/tool adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: As forefathers used stones, clubs or other weapons, they used their jaws and teeth less and the jaws and teeth would become reduced in size through selection, analogous to reduction of canines in male ruminants with horn development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider correlated effects (e.g., skull form altered by jaw-muscle size), and inheritance across sexes (reduction in males may affect females).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for changes in brain size and its interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The brain of man is larger in proportion to body than in apes and this large proportion is closely connected with higher mental powers; comparative and fossil evidence (skull capacities across races and over time) can support this link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: absolute skull volume is not a precise gauge of intellect—small nervous masses can correspond to complex behaviours (e.g., ants). Consider population effects (civilised vs savage averages), fossil comparisons, and relative vs absolute measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skull shape can be influenced by non-selective, developmental and cultural factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the skull may be modified by the kind of cradle, habitual head position due to trades, spasms, burns, or other developmental pressures; changes in body or brain size also alter skull shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing cranial differences to selection, control for environmental, mechanical, developmental and cultural influences (examples: elongated skull in some domestic rabbits due to selection or growth differences; human cranial differences possibly due to stature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating hypotheses for hair loss in humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple hypotheses exist: loss due to exposure to heat in tropical habitation, advantage of being destitute of hair to avoid parasites, or loss primarily by sexual selection (ornamental purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with other primates (many remain hairy despite tropical habitats), examine hair distribution patterns on human body and timing (loss before or after erect posture), and weigh parsimony and supporting observations (e.g., practices like singeing to remove vermin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining tail disappearance by mechanical injury and atrophy
rubrics_metrics.description: External disappearance of the tail in man and anthropomorphous apes may be due to the terminal portion being injured by friction (e.g., tail rubbed when sitting), causing atrophy and distortion over long periods; basal portion modified for support in erect posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed anatomical study of tail vertebrae (basal vs terminal portions), behavioural observations (Macacus brunneus sitting patterns causing tail wear), and knowledge of inherited effects of mutilations to evaluate this explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against over-attribution to natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of attributing too much to natural selection alone; other authors' criticisms (e.g., Nageli) and recent remarks suggest alternative or additional mechanisms may be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt pluralistic explanations: consider natural selection, sexual selection, use/disuse, correlated variation, developmental and environmental effects; reassess earlier attributions and remain open to revision in light of new evidence.
